newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: LEGAL WRANGLES STILL HAUNT SOUTH AFRICAN OIL RIG.
newsitem.headline: LEGAL WRANGLES STILL HAUNT SOUTH AFRICAN OIL RIG.

text.p: The fierce south-easter died down on Thursday but the Soekor-Energy Africa oil rig was still tied up in Simon's Town by legal wrangles.
Soekor project manager Andre van Niekerk told Reuters at mid-afternoon he believed the legal wrangle would be resolved "in a matter of hours rather than days."
"I doubt if we can still leave today...we need about six hours to get away from the quayside, so it is already too late for today," van Niekerk said.

The rig, the Orca, was "arrested" late on Monday by the sheriff's office due to a 31 million rand debt owed by French contractor Schlumberger, who has been refurbishing the rig, to local sub-contractor Babcock Construction.
This meant that the Orca was not able to leave for sea trials as scheduled on Tuesday.
But a strong south-easter also made departure impossible and it was hoped that the legal wrangle would be sorted out by Thursday, when the wind was expected to have died down.
"It's still in Simon's Town harbour and it looks as if we will be able to get her out here by tomorrow, hopefully," van Niekerk said.
After the sea trials, which will take about three days, the Orca will be towed to the Oribi oil field off Mossel Bay to start drilling South Africa's first offshore oilfield.
The Oribi oilfield is expected to initially produce 20,000 barrels of oil a day.
It will form the nucleus for the subsequent development of several other nearby oil discoveries, which would extend production life by a further six years.

Soekor and its 20 percent partner, Energy Africa Ltd, plan to pump the oil into a one million barrel shuttle tanker for shipment to one of South Africa's three coastal refineries in Cape Town or Durban.
